about: The scripted AI lesson for p5-newtons-laws (2026-11-28, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p5-forces-motion. Key point 1 says "the first law of motion": the word newton is taught in key point 2, where the laws are named after Isaac Newton.

keyPoints.heading: The first law of motion: resultant force and inertia

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about the three laws of motion: how forces change the way things move.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the last lesson. A car speeds up from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 s. What is its acceleration?
steps.right: Yes: acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s².

wrong.other: Not quite: 2 m/s².
wrong.times: Not quite: divide the change in velocity by the time: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s².
wrong.flip: Not quite: divide the change in velocity by the time, not the other way round: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 m/s².

idk.hint: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time. The velocity changes by 20 m/s in 10 s.

steps.answerWhy: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time = (20 − 0) ÷ 10 = 2 m/s².

steps.question: Second: which of these is a contact force?
steps.right: Yes: friction acts between surfaces that touch.

wrong.other: Not quite: friction.
wrong.gravity: Not quite: gravity acts across a gap, so it is a non-contact force. Friction needs surfaces that touch.
wrong.magnet: Not quite: magnetic force acts across a gap, so it is a non-contact force. Friction needs surfaces that touch.

idk.hint: A contact force needs the objects to touch.

steps.answerWhy: Friction acts between surfaces that touch, so it is a contact force.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Most objects have several forces on them at once. A box on the floor is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the floor.
Forces are measured in a unit written N. Its name comes in the next part of the lesson.
You can replace all the forces on an object with one force that has the same effect. That single force is called the resultant force.
For forces along one line, add the forces that act the same way and take away those that act the opposite way. For example, 50 N forwards and 20 N backwards make 30 N forwards.

steps.question: A sledge is pulled forwards with 60 N, and friction pulls it back with 25 N. What is the size of the resultant force, in N?
steps.right: Yes: 60 − 25 = 35 N, forwards.

wrong.other: Not quite: 35 N. The forces act opposite ways, so subtract: 60 − 25 = 35 N, forwards.
wrong.add: Not quite: 35 N. The forces act in opposite directions, so subtract them: 60 − 25 = 35 N.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 35 N. Forces in opposite directions are subtracted: 60 − 25 = 35 N.

idk.hint: The two forces act in opposite directions. Take the smaller from the bigger.

steps.answerWhy: The forces act in opposite directions, so the resultant is 60 − 25 = 35 N, in the direction of the bigger force.

steps.question: Two people pull a box in opposite directions, each with a force of 40 N. What is the resultant force on the box?
steps.right: Yes: 40 − 40 = 0 N. The forces cancel.

wrong.other: Not quite: 0 N.
wrong.add: Not quite: the forces act in opposite directions, so subtract them: 40 − 40 = 0 N.
wrong.one: Not quite: each pull is 40 N, but they act in opposite directions and cancel: 0 N.

idk.hint: The two forces are the same size and act opposite ways. What is 40 − 40?

steps.answerWhy: The forces are equal and opposite, so the resultant is 40 − 40 = 0 N.

steps.text: When the resultant force is zero, the forces are balanced. Balanced does not mean there are no forces: they are there, but they cancel.

The first law of motion says: if the resultant force on an object is zero, a still object stays still, and a moving object keeps the same velocity. It works the other way too: steady velocity means zero resultant force.
In everyday life, moving things do slow down and stop. That is because friction and air resistance, the push of the air on moving things, act on them, so the resultant force is not zero.

steps.question: A car drives along a straight, level road at a steady 25 m/s. What is the resultant force on it?

options.text: Zero: the forces on it balance
Forwards: it needs one to keep going
There are no forces on it

steps.right: Yes: its velocity is not changing, so the resultant force is zero.

wrong.other: Not quite: zero.
wrong.keepgoing: Not quite: a moving object keeps the same velocity with no resultant force. The driving force only balances the friction and air resistance holding it back.
wrong.none: Not quite: there are forces on it, such as the driving force and air resistance. They balance, so the resultant is zero.

idk.hint: Steady speed in a straight line means the velocity is not changing. With no change in velocity, what must the resultant force be?

steps.answerWhy: The car's velocity is not changing, so by the first law the resultant force is zero: the forces balance.

steps.text: Changing the speed or the direction of an object needs a resultant force.

steps.question: You push a trolley with a steady force. On carpet, it moves at a steady speed. It then rolls onto smooth tiles, where friction is smaller, and you keep pushing the same. Which is true on the tiles?
steps.right: Yes: the push is now bigger than the friction, so there is a forward resultant force and the trolley speeds up.

wrong.other: Not quite: it speeds up.
wrong.same: Not quite: on the carpet the push and friction balanced. On the tiles friction is smaller, so there is a forward resultant force and it speeds up.
wrong.slow: Not quite: less friction means less force holding it back. The push wins, so the resultant is forwards and it speeds up.

idk.hint: On the tiles, the push is bigger than the friction, so the resultant force acts forwards. A forward resultant force changes the speed. Which way?

steps.answerWhy: With less friction, the push is bigger than the friction, so the resultant force acts forwards and the trolley speeds up.

steps.text: Objects tend to keep doing what they are already doing: staying still, or moving at a steady velocity. This tendency is called inertia.
The more mass an object has, the more inertia it has. A lorry is much harder to start or stop than a bicycle.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does the first law of motion say?
points: With zero resultant force, an object keeps the same velocity, or stays still
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: if the resultant force on an object is zero, a still object stays still and a moving object keeps the same speed and direction.

steps.text: The N stands for the newton, the unit of force, named after the scientist Isaac Newton. The three laws of motion are his, so they are called Newton's laws.

The second law tells you how big the acceleration is. The bigger the resultant force, the bigger the acceleration. The bigger the mass, the amount of matter in the object, the smaller the acceleration.
The equation is F = m a: resultant force = mass × acceleration. Here F is the resultant force in newtons (N), m is the mass in kilograms (kg) and a is the acceleration in m/s².
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 3 m/s². What resultant force acts on it?
steps: Write the equation: F = m a.

steps.text: F = m a can be rearranged: a = F ÷ m to find the acceleration, and m = F ÷ a to find the mass.

steps.question: Your turn. A 0.5 kg ball is given an acceleration of 8 m/s². What resultant force acts on it, in N?

wrong.other: Not quite: 4 N. F = m a = 0.5 × 8 = 4 N.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 4 N. Multiply the mass by the acceleration: 0.5 × 8 = 4 N.
wrong.square: Not quite: 4 N. The "squared" in m/s² is part of the unit. Do not square the 8: F = 0.5 × 8 = 4 N.
wrong.flip: Not quite: 4 N. Multiply the mass by the acceleration: 0.5 × 8 = 4 N.

idk.hint: Force = mass × acceleration. Multiply 0.5 by 8.

steps.question: Now find an acceleration. A resultant force of 150 N acts on a 50 kg crate. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?

wrong.other: Not quite: 3 m/s². Rearrange F = m a to a = F ÷ m = 150 ÷ 50 = 3 m/s².
wrong.times: Not quite: 3 m/s². To find a, divide the force by the mass: 150 ÷ 50 = 3 m/s².
wrong.flip: Not quite: 3 m/s². Divide the force by the mass, not the mass by the force: 150 ÷ 50 = 3 m/s².

idk.hint: Rearrange F = m a to get a = F ÷ m.

steps.text: Mass measured as force ÷ acceleration, m = F ÷ a, is called inertial mass: it measures how hard an object is to accelerate.

steps.question: The same resultant force acts on an empty shopping trolley and on a full one. Which has the bigger acceleration?
steps.right: Yes: the empty trolley has less mass, so the same force gives it a bigger acceleration.

wrong.other: Not quite: the empty trolley.
wrong.full: Not quite: more mass means less acceleration for the same force, because a = F ÷ m. The empty trolley accelerates more.
wrong.same: Not quite: a = F ÷ m, so with the same force, the smaller mass has the bigger acceleration: the empty trolley.

idk.hint: a = F ÷ m. With the same F, which trolley has the smaller m?

steps.answerWhy: a = F ÷ m, so with the same force the trolley with less mass, the empty one, has the bigger acceleration.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does F = m a tell you?
points: A bigger resultant force gives a bigger acceleration
A bigger mass gives a smaller acceleration
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: F = m a tells you a bigger resultant force gives a bigger acceleration, and a bigger mass a smaller one.

steps.text: The third law is about two objects pushing or pulling on each other. When object A pushes on object B, B pushes back on A with a force of the same size, in the opposite direction.
The two forces are the same kind of force, such as both pushes or both gravity, and they act on different objects. Together they are called a Newton's third law pair.

steps.question: You push on a wall with a force of 30 N. What force does the wall push on you with?

options.text: Less than 30 N, as it does not move

steps.right: Yes: the wall pushes back on you with 30 N.

wrong.other: Not quite: 30 N, back towards you.
wrong.none: Not quite: the wall does push. By the third law, it pushes back on you with 30 N.
wrong.less: Not quite: the two forces in a pair are always the same size, so the wall pushes back with 30 N.

idk.hint: The third law says the two forces in a pair are the same size and opposite in direction.

steps.answerWhy: By the third law, the wall pushes back on you with a force of the same size, 30 N, in the opposite direction.

steps.text: A third law pair never cancels out. Only forces acting on the same object can cancel.

steps.question: A rocket engine pushes hot gas downwards. Which force pushes the rocket up?

options.text: The gas pushing up on the engine
The air below pushing up on it

steps.right: Yes: the engine pushes the gas down, so the gas pushes the engine up.

wrong.other: Not quite: the gas pushing up on the engine.
wrong.air: Not quite: rockets work in space too, where there is no air. The engine pushes the gas down, so the gas pushes the engine up.
wrong.gravity: Not quite: gravity pulls things down, not up. The engine pushes the gas down, so the gas pushes the engine up.

idk.hint: The engine pushes on the gas. By the third law, what pushes back on the engine?

steps.answerWhy: The engine pushes the gas down, so by the third law the gas pushes the engine up with a force of the same size.

steps.text: Even gravity comes in pairs. The Earth pulls you down, and you pull the Earth up with a force just as big. The Earth's mass is so huge that your pull hardly moves it.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does the third law of motion say?
points: When two objects interact, they push or pull on each other with equal and opposite forces
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: when two objects interact, each pushes or pulls on the other with a force of the same size in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.heading: Weight, mass and free body diagrams

steps.text: The pull of gravity on an object is called weight. Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons.
How strongly gravity pulls on each kilogram is called the gravitational field strength, g.
Gravitational field strength is measured in newtons per kilogram (N/kg). On Earth, g is about 9.8 N/kg.
The equation is W = m g: weight = mass × gravitational field strength. Here W is the weight in newtons (N), m is the mass in kilograms (kg) and g is in N/kg. In a question, you are given g.
Mass stays the same everywhere, but weight changes with g. On the Moon g is about 1.6 N/kg, so you weigh about a sixth as much there.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A 70 kg person stands on Earth, where g = 9.8 N/kg. What is their weight?
steps: Write the equation: W = m g.

steps.question: A bag has a mass of 5 kg, and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is its weight, in N?

wrong.other: Not quite: 49 N. W = m g = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 49 N. Multiply the mass by g: 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.
wrong.add: Not quite: 49 N. Multiply the mass by g, do not add them: 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.

idk.hint: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength. Multiply 5 by 9.8.

steps.question: An apple has a mass of 200 g, and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is its weight, in N? (1000 g = 1 kg.)

wrong.grams: Not quite: 1.96 N. Change grams into kilograms first: 200 g = 0.2 kg. Then 0.2 × 9.8 = 1.96 N.

idk.hint: Change 200 g into kilograms first: 1000 g = 1 kg.

steps.text: Weight and mass are directly proportional: double the mass, and the weight doubles.
Weight is measured with a newtonmeter: a spring balance marked in newtons.
An object's weight can be treated as acting at one point, called its centre of mass. A ruler balances on your finger when your finger is under its centre of mass.
A diagram that shows one object with every force on it, each as a labelled arrow, is called a free body diagram. Longer arrows show bigger forces.
For a book resting on a table, the free body diagram has two arrows of the same length: its weight down, and the push up from the table, called the normal contact force. The resultant force is zero.

steps.question: A free body diagram of a falling skydiver shows a 600 N weight down and 450 N of air resistance, the push of the air, up. What is the resultant force?
steps.right: Yes: 600 − 450 = 150 N, downwards, the way the bigger force acts.

wrong.other: Not quite: 150 N downwards.
wrong.add: Not quite: the forces act in opposite directions, so subtract: 600 − 450 = 150 N, downwards.
wrong.dir: Not quite: the size is right, but the bigger force, the weight, acts downwards. So the resultant is 150 N downwards.

idk.hint: The forces act in opposite directions. Subtract them, and the resultant points the way of the bigger one.

steps.answerWhy: The resultant is 600 − 450 = 150 N, in the direction of the bigger force: downwards.

steps.text: Forces that are not in a line can be added with a scale drawing. Draw each force as an arrow to scale, tip to tail. The arrow from the start of the first to the end of the last is the resultant.
A scale drawing can also split one force into two parts at right angles, such as along the ground and upwards. Together, the two parts have the same effect as the one force.

steps.question: A rope pulls a sledge forwards and upwards at a slant. Split into two parts at right angles, which pair does the same job as the pull?

options.text: A part along the ground and a part upwards
Two parts, both along the ground
A part along the rope and a part backwards

steps.right: Yes: one part pulls the sledge along the ground and one lifts it a little. Together they have the same effect as the pull.

wrong.other: Not quite: a part along the ground and a part upwards.
wrong.both: Not quite: the two parts must be at right angles to each other: one along the ground and one upwards.
wrong.back: Not quite: the two parts must be at right angles, and together do the same job as the pull: one along the ground and one upwards.

idk.hint: The two parts are at right angles to each other. The pull is partly forwards and partly upwards.

steps.answerWhy: The slanted pull can be split into a part along the ground and a part upwards, at right angles, which together have the same effect.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is weight, and how do you work it out?
points: Weight is the force of gravity on an object
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: weight is the force of gravity on an object: weight = mass × gravitational field strength.

keyPoints.heading: Required practical: force, mass and acceleration

steps.text: Now a class practical that tests the second law: how force and mass change the acceleration.
In a class experiment, a trolley on a bench is pulled by a string that runs over a pulley, a wheel at the edge of the bench, to masses hanging on the end.
Light gates are electronic timers. They time the trolley, so its acceleration can be worked out.
The pull on the trolley comes from the hanging masses. To make the pull bigger, masses are moved from the trolley onto the hanging end.

steps.question: Why are masses moved from the trolley, rather than new masses added?

options.text: To keep the total mass being pulled the same
To make the trolley go faster
To stop the string from breaking

steps.right: Yes: moving masses changes the force but keeps the total mass the same, so only one thing changes.

wrong.other: Not quite: to keep the total mass being pulled the same.
wrong.faster: Not quite: the point is a fair test. Moving masses keeps the total mass the same, so only the force changes.
wrong.string: Not quite: the string is fine either way. Moving masses keeps the total mass the same, so only the force changes.

idk.hint: Mass also changes the acceleration. Adding new masses would change the total mass. Moving them does not.

steps.answerWhy: Moving masses from the trolley to the hanging end changes the force but keeps the total mass the same, so only the force changes.

steps.text: The quantity you change on purpose is called the independent variable. In the first part of the practical, that is the force.
The quantity you measure is the dependent variable: here, the acceleration. A quantity you keep the same on purpose is called a control variable.

steps.question: In the first part, the force goes up and the total mass stays the same. What do you think the graph of acceleration against force looks like?

options.text: A straight line through the origin
A flat line: the acceleration stays the same

steps.right: Yes: a straight line through the origin. So the acceleration is directly proportional to the force: a ∝ F.

wrong.other: Not quite: a straight line through the origin.
wrong.flat: Not quite: a bigger resultant force gives a bigger acceleration, so the line goes up. It is a straight line through the origin: a ∝ F.
wrong.down: Not quite: more force gives more acceleration, not less. The line is straight and goes through the origin: a ∝ F.

idk.hint: F = m a with m kept the same. If F doubles, what happens to a?

steps.answerWhy: With the mass kept the same, doubling the force doubles the acceleration, so the graph is a straight line through the origin: a ∝ F.

steps.text: In the second part, the hanging masses stay the same, so the force is constant. Masses are added to the trolley, and the acceleration is measured each time.

steps.question: With more mass on the trolley and the same pull, which is true of the acceleration?
steps.right: Yes: the same force on more mass gives less acceleration.

wrong.other: Not quite: it gets smaller.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: a = F ÷ m, so with the same force, more mass means less acceleration.
wrong.same: Not quite: a = F ÷ m, so with the same force, more mass means less acceleration.

idk.hint: a = F ÷ m. With F the same, what does a bigger m do?

steps.answerWhy: a = F ÷ m, so with the force kept the same, more mass gives a smaller acceleration.

steps.prompt: In one line: what does the trolley practical show?
points: With the mass kept the same, the acceleration is directly proportional to the force
With the force kept the same, more mass gives less acceleration
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: the trolley practical shows that acceleration is directly proportional to force when the mass stays the same, and that more mass gives less acceleration for the same force.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: 80 N pushes a box to the right and 30 N pushes it to the left. What is the resultant force?
steps.right: Yes: 80 − 30 = 50 N, to the right.

wrong.other: Not quite: 50 N to the right.
wrong.add: Not quite: opposite forces are subtracted: 80 − 30 = 50 N, to the right.
wrong.dir: Not quite: the bigger force acts to the right, so the resultant does too: 50 N to the right.

idk.hint: Opposite forces: subtract, then take the direction of the bigger force.

steps.answerWhy: 80 − 30 = 50 N, in the direction of the bigger force: to the right.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: the resultant force on a moving ball is zero. Which is true?
steps.right: Yes: with no resultant force, its speed and direction stay the same.

wrong.other: Not quite: it keeps the same velocity.
wrong.stop: Not quite: slowing down needs a resultant force backwards. With zero resultant, it keeps the same velocity.
wrong.faster: Not quite: speeding up needs a resultant force forwards. With zero resultant, it keeps the same velocity.

idk.hint: Think of the first law of motion.

steps.answerWhy: By the first law, a zero resultant force means the velocity does not change.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: a 2 kg mass accelerates at 3 m/s². What is the resultant force on it?
steps.right: Yes: F = m a = 2 × 3 = 6 N.

wrong.other: Not quite: 6 N.
wrong.divide: Not quite: multiply the mass by the acceleration: 2 × 3 = 6 N.
wrong.add: Not quite: multiply, do not add: 2 × 3 = 6 N.

idk.hint: F = m a.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: a book pushes down on a table. Which force is the other one in its third law pair?

options.text: The table pushing up on the book
The floor pushing up on the table

steps.right: Yes: the pair is the book on the table and the table on the book.

wrong.other: Not quite: the table pushing up on the book.
wrong.weight: Not quite: the weight is gravity pulling on the book, a different type of force. The pair is the table pushing up on the book.
wrong.floor: Not quite: that force is between the floor and the table. The pair is the table pushing up on the book.

idk.hint: In a pair, the same two objects push on each other.

steps.answerWhy: A third law pair is between the same two objects: the book pushes on the table, and the table pushes up on the book.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: what is the weight of a 10 kg mass where g = 9.8 N/kg?

wrong.other: Not quite: 98 N.
wrong.mass: Not quite: 10 kg is the mass. The weight is W = m g = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.
wrong.divide: Not quite: multiply the mass by g: 10 × 9.8 = 98 N.

idk.hint: W = m g.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: in the trolley practical, the force changes and the total mass stays the same. What is the total mass?
steps.right: Yes: it is kept the same on purpose, so it is a control variable.

wrong.other: Not quite: a control variable.
wrong.indep: Not quite: the independent variable is what you change on purpose, the force. The total mass is kept the same: a control variable.
wrong.dep: Not quite: the dependent variable is what you measure, the acceleration. The total mass is kept the same: a control variable.

idk.hint: Is the total mass changed, measured, or kept the same on purpose?

steps.answerWhy: The total mass is kept the same on purpose, so it is a control variable.

steps.text: That's the end of the quiz: you got {right} out of {n}.

end.text: The lesson is finished. Tap a button to go on.
